newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr fails to capitalise on breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr fails to capitalise on breakthrough.

text.p: The Australian dollar finally escaped its week-old range Tuesday, but failed to make a clean getaway and by the close was on the cusp of recapture.

Asian and European buying Monday had seen a local short squeeze snowball into a stop loss bidding spree which carried it 1/2 cent higher to a US$0.7823 peak overnight. However, U.S. sales reined it back to US$0.7790 support where offers and bids found a temporary balance.
The failure to maintain momentum disappointed long suffering bulls and left the currency vulnerable should U.S. wages data tonight heighten the risk of a Federal Reserve rate hike.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was back in all too familiar territory at US$0.7790/95 having eased from an early US$0.7800/05 and a US$0.7823 peak overnight.

That was still up on Monday's late US$0.7770/75 but dealers felt it needed to finish the New York session atop 78 cents to convince a sceptical market the rally was anymore than a blip. The loss of US$0.7765, on the other hand, would brand the bounce as false and see US$0.7720 support re-tested.
On the crosses the dollar had benefited from sizeable German and Japanese demand offshore, although the latter dried up today as Tokyo was off on holiday.

As a result the dollar was up at 1.3489/01 marks from 1.3458/70 late Monday but pared its gains on the yen to end at 98.67/77 from 98.50/60. In trade weighted terms it was still firmer at 60.6 from a previous 60.4 close.

There were no domestic data to provide direction today and Wednesday's reading on the balance of goods and services for March was unlikely to contribute much to the debate over monetary policy -- the market's present obsession.
Median forecasts for this measure, which replaced the highly volatile monthly current account figures, is for a surplus of A$150 million down slightly from February's A$336 million.
For the market, Q1 average weekly earnings data on Thursday will be far more meaningful since the pace of wages growth revealed may prove an impediment to another rate cut.
Forecasts center on a year on year riseof 4.3 percent from 3.9 in Q4 but estimates go as high as 4.6 percent which would put wages growth in the RBA's 4.5-5.0 percent danger zone.
Figures on U.S. wages due out tonight may also have implications for Australian/U.S. interest differentials.
The employment cost index has been singled out by the Federal Reserve as a reliable indicator of labour costs and so is closely watched by the market.
The indicator had been surprisingly subdued during 1996 but analysts are looking for signs of upward pressure to show from the tightening labour market and from rising benefit costs.
Median forecasts favour a rise of 0.9 percent in Q1 which would take annual growth to 3.1 percent from 2.8 percent in Q4.

Some analysts see the risk on the upside given anecdotal evidence of rising health care premiums and expect a gain of more than 1.0 percent. Such a rise would harden expectations the Fed would tighten policy again at its next meeting on May 20 and would likely see the A$'s yield advantage over the U.S. dollar erode further. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
